modules.title: How the body uses daily inputs

concepts.title: Protein in everyday food
concepts.hook: ICMR-NIN notes that cereals and pulses can complement each other’s amino acids.
concepts.rule: Protein comes from many foods. Pulses and cereals together give a good mix of key amino acids. No one food has to supply all we need.

claims.text: Cereals or millets and pulses can fill gaps in each other’s amino acid mix.

items.stem: At a college canteen, dal is served with rice. What does the dal bring that rice alone supplies less of?

options.feedback: ICMR-NIN names pulses as protein-rich plant foods.
Dal is a pulse; pulses supply protein. That makes dal part of the meal's protein mix.

options.text: Mostly vitamin C to go with the rice.
options.feedback: Dal is valued here as a pulse with protein. Vitamin C comes mostly from fruit and fresh vegetables.

items.stem: A school cook pairs a millet with chana. Why can that pairing be useful?

options.text: Their amino-acid profiles complement each other.
options.feedback: ICMR-NIN describes the cereal or millet and pulse combination.

options.text: The foods become a new vitamin.
options.feedback: Mixing food groups does not create a vitamin.
The pulse is itself protein-rich. The pulse adds protein to the meal as well.

items.stem: Which food pair fits the ICMR-NIN guide for protein?

options.text: Cereal or millet with a pulse.
options.feedback: The guide says these groups complement one another.
That can be a meal, but it misses the specific complementary pairing.

options.text: Only a sweet drink with a cereal.
options.feedback: A sweet drink does not play the pulse role in this example.

items.stem: A poster says a meal with no meat cannot give useful protein. What is wrong?

options.text: Pulses and other plant foods provide protein.
options.feedback: The guide says pulses can give protein. They can pair well with grains.

options.text: Every plant food has the same amino acids.
options.feedback: The reason to vary groups is that their profiles differ.

options.text: Cereal and pulse pairing removes all need for variety.
options.feedback: Foods can fill gaps in each other’s amino acid mix. A varied diet helps too.

items.stem: According to ICMR-NIN, one gram of protein supplies about how much energy?

options.feedback: The guideline gives protein energy as 4 kcal per gram.
That is a common figure for fat, not protein.
Protein gives the body energy. It also helps build and mend tissue.

items.stem: A menu gives rice but says dal adds no nutritional value. What is missing?

options.text: Dal adds protein and a different amino-acid mix.
options.feedback: That is why ICMR-NIN highlights cereal-pulse combinations.

options.text: Rice has no nutrients at all.
options.feedback: The two foods fill gaps in each other’s amino acid mix. Rice is not empty of protein.

options.text: Dal works only when meat is also served.
options.feedback: The guide gives cereal-pulse pairing as a plant-food example.

items.stem: Build the logic of a cereal-pulse protein pairing.

options.feedback: This is one protein-containing food group. Cereals and pulses can both add protein to a meal.
Pulses add a different amino-acid profile. That can help fill gaps in the cereal's amino acids.
The groups complement each other. Each group brings amino acids the other has less of.

items.stem: Match each food to its group.

options.feedback: A protein-rich legume. Chana is a pulse, so it adds protein to the meal.
A protein-rich legume. This is why chana can add protein to a meal.
A grain that can pair with a pulse.
A grain that can pair with a pulse.

misconceptions.name: Plant foods lack protein
misconceptions.correction: Pulses are a substantial plant source of protein.

misconceptions.name: One meal needs a perfect protein
misconceptions.correction: A varied diet can draw amino acids from different foods.

quest.title: Spot the mix
quest.detail: Look at a familiar meal and name its pulse, cereal or other protein foods.

concepts.title: Free sugars
concepts.hook: Fruit juice counts toward WHO’s free-sugar guidance even when no spoonful of sugar was added.
concepts.rule: WHO free sugars include added sugar, honey, syrups and fruit juice sugars. On a 2,000-kcal day, below 10% of energy is about 50 g; 5% or less may add benefit.

claims.text: WHO includes honey, syrups and fruit juice sugars in free sugars, but excludes the sugars in whole fresh fruit.
WHO says free sugars should give less than 10% of daily energy. At 5% or less, there may be more benefit.

items.stem: A school drink is sweetened with honey instead of table sugar. Does it escape the WHO free sugar rule?

options.feedback: WHO explicitly includes honey. Its source does not put it outside the free sugar rule.

options.text: Yes; only refined white sugar counts.
options.feedback: WHO’s definition covers more than white sugar.

options.text: Yes, if the honey is raw and local.
options.feedback: WHO counts the sugars in honey whether it is raw, local or processed. Where it comes from does not change the rule.

items.stem: At a college canteen, a glass of fruit juice and a whole orange contain fruit sugars. Which has free sugars under the WHO rule?

options.feedback: WHO names fruit juice; sugars held in whole fruit are treated differently.

options.text: Both in exactly the same way.
options.feedback: The definition singles out juice, not intact whole fruit.

options.text: Neither, because both began as fruit.
options.feedback: Juice sugars still count as free sugars, even when the juice comes from fruit.

items.stem: Which source is within WHO’s free-sugar category?

options.feedback: Syrups are named in the definition. That is why sugar from syrup counts as free sugar.
Starch in rice is not free sugar. The rule concerns added sugars, not all starch in food.

options.text: The sugars inside an intact apple.
options.feedback: Whole fruit is outside this definition. Its sugars stay within the whole fruit, unlike juice sugars.

items.stem: A package says “no added sugar,” yet contains fruit juice concentrate. Why check it?

options.text: Juice concentrate still brings free sugars.
options.feedback: WHO includes sugars in fruit juice concentrates. The source of the sugar still puts it in this group.

options.text: The claim proves the drink has zero sugar.
options.feedback: No added sugar does not mean no free sugars.

options.text: Whole fruit and juice concentrate are identical categories.
options.feedback: WHO draws a distinction between juice and intact fruit.

items.stem: For a 2,000-kcal day, WHO equates its below-10% free-sugar guidance to about how many grams?

options.feedback: WHO gives this approximate conversion for a 2,000-kcal day.
Five is the further-benefit percentage, not this gram figure.
That would be far above the stated energy share.

items.stem: Someone says WHO’s 5% figure replaced the 10% limit for everyone. Which reading is closer?

options.text: Below 10% is the main limit; 5% or less may bring more benefit.
options.feedback: WHO states both levels with different roles. The lower level is a further aim, not the main cap.

options.text: Ten percent refers to all carbohydrates.
options.feedback: The WHO rule is about free sugars. It does not count all carbs in food.

options.text: Five percent means five grams a day.
options.feedback: A percentage of energy is not a fixed gram amount across diets.

items.stem: Check whether a sweet source enters WHO’s free-sugar category.

options.feedback: The source matters for this definition. Added sugar and juice count, while whole fruit does not.

options.text: Check for added sugar, honey, syrup or juice.
options.feedback: WHO includes these sources. Honey and syrup count even when they sound natural.
Its intrinsic sugars are not counted as free sugars.

items.stem: Match each food to its WHO category.

options.feedback: WHO explicitly includes juice sugars. Juice is one of the sources named in the rule.
WHO explicitly includes juice sugars. Those sugars count even when the juice has no added sugar.
Whole fruit is treated differently from juice. Its sugars remain inside the fruit, unlike those in juice.
Whole fruit is treated differently from juice. That is the name for sugars held inside whole fruit.

misconceptions.name: Natural sweeteners are exempt
misconceptions.correction: Honey and juice sugars count as free sugars.

misconceptions.name: All fruit sugar is free sugar
misconceptions.correction: The guidance treats whole fruit differently from juice.

quest.title: Read a drink label
quest.detail: Find a drink label and note its sugar entry. Ask whether sugar was added or came from juice.

concepts.title: Hydration cues
concepts.hook: NHS counts tea and milk as fluid, and calls its six-to-eight-cup figure a guide.
concepts.rule: Water is a useful drink, but other drinks and some foods add fluid. Heat and long activity can change needs, so one cup count does not fit every day.

claims.text: NHS gives six to eight cups or glasses of fluid as a general guide, not a fixed water-only rule.
Tea, coffee, milk and foods can add fluid; hot settings and long activity can raise needs.

items.stem: At school, a student drinks milk with breakfast. Does NHS count it toward fluid intake?

options.feedback: NHS lists lower-fat milk among drinks that count.
That ignores other drinks in the NHS guide.

options.text: No, milk counts as food, not fluid.
options.feedback: Milk is mostly water. The NHS lists lower-fat milk among the drinks that count toward fluid.

items.stem: After a long walk in hot weather, a college student checks the six to eight cup guide. Is it an exact cap?

options.text: No; heat and long activity can raise fluid needs.
options.feedback: NHS names both reasons needs may change. Hot weather and long activity can call for more fluid.

options.text: Yes; eight cups is a safe maximum for all adults.
options.feedback: The NHS calls it a guide, not a universal cap.

options.text: The walk matters only if no food was eaten.
options.feedback: Heat and a long walk can change fluid needs. Meal time does not set the guide.

items.stem: Which of these adds fluid, as the NHS guide says?

options.feedback: NHS counts tea and notes that food also supplies some fluid.
That leaves out other drinks and food. Other drinks and fluid in food can count too.
Flavour is not the criterion in the NHS account.

items.stem: Why is the “exactly eight glasses of water” rule too rigid?

options.text: It mistakes a fluid guide for a fixed water-only target.
options.feedback: The NHS guide includes other drinks and variable conditions.

options.text: Because no one ever needs fluid from drinks.
options.feedback: Drinks remain an important source of fluid. The guide counts drinks as a main way to get fluid.

options.text: Because tea always cancels water intake.
options.feedback: NHS counts tea toward the daily fluid total.

items.stem: What is the lower end of the NHS hydration guide of six to eight daily cups or glasses of fluid?

options.feedback: The NHS range starts at six and remains a guide.
Eight is the upper end of a fluid range, not its lower end or a water-only rule.
That is outside the general range on the NHS page.

items.stem: A chart lists water but excludes coffee from all fluid totals. What should change?

options.text: Coffee can count as fluid too.
options.feedback: NHS includes lower-sugar drinks such as coffee.

options.text: Coffee and water are identical in every respect.
options.feedback: Both contribute fluid, but their other properties differ.

options.text: Only hot coffee counts, not cold coffee.
options.feedback: Temperature is not what makes it a fluid.

items.stem: Read a hydration guide in context.

options.text: Start with the general fluid range.
options.feedback: NHS offers a starting guide. It is a guide for most people, not an exact cap.

options.text: Count drinks and some food fluid.
options.feedback: Plain water is not the only contribution. Milk and tea can add fluid to a day as well.

options.text: Adjust for heat or long activity.
options.feedback: Those conditions can change needs. So the same cup guide may not fit every day.

items.stem: Pair each clue with its implication.

options.feedback: NHS includes these drinks. Tea and milk can add to the day's fluid intake.
NHS includes these drinks. They count toward fluid intake, even without plain water.
The guide allows for hotter conditions. A hot day may mean the usual guide is too low.
The guide allows for hotter conditions. The body can need more fluid when it is hot.

misconceptions.name: Only plain water counts
misconceptions.correction: Other drinks and some foods contribute fluid.

misconceptions.name: Eight glasses fits everyone
misconceptions.correction: The NHS figure is a guide that changes with conditions.

quest.title: Notice fluids
quest.detail: For one meal, name the drink and any food that brings fluid, with no target to meet.

concepts.title: Sleep and recovery
concepts.hook: Sleep is active: the brain cycles through stages while the body carries out repair.
concepts.rule: Adults generally need seven or more hours of sleep. Sleep quality and repeating stages also matter; deep sleep tends to be longer earlier in the night.

claims.text: CDC recommends seven or more hours of sleep for adults aged 18–60.
NIH describes cycling sleep stages and more deep sleep earlier in the night.

items.stem: A school chart shows deep and REM sleep stages. What does that reveal?

options.feedback: NIH describes repeating non-REM and REM stages.

options.text: The brain is switched off throughout.
options.feedback: REM and other stages involve brain activity. The brain does different work as sleep stages change.

options.text: Most deep sleep comes just before waking.
options.feedback: Deep sleep tends to be longer early in the night. REM spells grow longer toward morning.

items.stem: A college student hears that everyone needs exactly five hours of sleep. What is closer to CDC guidance?

options.text: Adults aged 18–60 generally need seven or more hours.
options.feedback: CDC gives seven or more hours for that age band.

options.text: Five hours is the CDC target for all adults.
options.feedback: That is below the stated general recommendation. CDC says most adults in this age group need more.

options.text: The number of hours never varies with age.
options.feedback: CDC lists different ranges for different ages. A child and an adult can have different sleep needs.

items.stem: Which stage tends to last longer in the first half of the night?

options.feedback: NIH places more deep sleep earlier in the night.
REM is part of sleep, but deep sleep is the stage emphasized early.
The question concerns a sleep stage, not awake time.

items.stem: Why can a full night include several distinct patterns on a sleep study?

options.feedback: A changing pattern fits the NIH account of cycles.

options.text: One stage must last without interruption until morning.
options.feedback: The stages recur rather than forming one unbroken block.

options.text: No brain activity occurs during REM.
options.feedback: REM is associated with active brain patterns. The brain stays active during this part of sleep.

items.stem: For adult sleep, what minimum nightly hours does CDC list for ages 18 to 60?

options.feedback: CDC gives seven or more for this adult age band.
That falls below the general CDC recommendation. CDC lists seven or more hours for adults aged 18 to 60.
That is above the stated lower bound, not its value.

items.stem: A claim says deep sleep lasts all night, so REM can be skipped in a diagram. What is wrong?

options.text: A normal night includes both non-REM and REM stages.
options.feedback: NIH describes cycles through more than deep sleep.

options.text: Deep sleep is absent early in the night.
options.feedback: It often lasts longer in the first half.
REM is itself a sleep stage. That makes it part of the night, not waking time.

items.stem: Trace a simplified sleep-stage cycle.

options.feedback: The early cycle starts with lighter sleep. This stage comes before deeper sleep and REM sleep.
Deep sleep is one later non-REM stage.

options.text: REM sleep appears later in the cycle.
options.feedback: The stages can repeat through the night. Sleep can cycle through them more than once.

items.stem: Pair each source statement with its meaning.

options.feedback: The age band is 18–60. CDC gives this guide for adults aged 18 to 60.
The age band is 18–60. It is a guide for that adult age group.
The night is not one blank block. The brain and body change as the stages repeat.
The night is not one blank block. The stages repeat, with changes in brain activity.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is a blank state
misconceptions.correction: Sleep has stages. They repeat, and the brain acts in new ways in each stage.

misconceptions.name: One short night defines a person
misconceptions.correction: The adult guidance is a population guide, not a diagnosis from one night.

sources.title: About Sleep
sources.publisher: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

quest.title: Draw a sleep wave
quest.detail: Draw a simple wave of light, deep and REM sleep. Mark where deep sleep tends to be longer.

concepts.title: Exercise and the heart
concepts.hook: WHO says adults can build up time spent on walks and other moves each week. A brisk walk can count.
concepts.rule: A brisk walk makes the heart and lungs work more. WHO says adults can aim for 150 to 300 minutes of such work each week. Some is better than none.

claims.text: WHO says adults can aim for 150 to 300 minutes of brisk walks or other moderate aerobic work each week.
Moves done often can help the heart. Some is better than none.

items.stem: A college student takes a brisk walk. Which activity category can it fit?

options.feedback: WHO uses brisk walking as an example of moderate movement.
Brisk walking need not be a sprint to count.

options.text: Light movement that does not count at all.
options.feedback: WHO uses a brisk walk as its example of moderate work. It counts toward the 150 to 300 weekly minutes.

items.stem: A school friend has less time than the WHO weekly range. Is some walking still meaningful?

options.text: Yes; some activity is better than none.
options.feedback: WHO explicitly says this while giving the weekly range.

options.text: No; anything below 150 minutes has no benefit.
options.feedback: The range is a recommendation, not an on-off switch.
Walking for transport or leisure can count too.

items.stem: How much brisk walk time does WHO list for adults in one week?

options.feedback: That is the WHO recommended range. It applies to moderate aerobic activity in a week.
This drops a zero from both ends of the weekly range.
WHO does not set that as the standard range.

items.stem: Why can brisk walking support heart health over time?

options.text: It is repeated aerobic movement that works the heart.
options.feedback: When muscles move, the heart has more work to do. Walks done often can help health.

options.text: The heart stops pumping during a walk.
options.feedback: Active muscles require continued blood flow. Working muscles still need blood while someone walks.

options.text: Only the speed of a sprint can affect the heart.
options.feedback: Moderate aerobic activity also counts. A brisk walk can raise the heart's work too.

items.stem: What is the lower end of the WHO weekly moderate exercise range for adults?

options.feedback: WHO gives 150–300 minutes as its adult range.
That is for harder work. WHO gives more time for brisk walks and other moderate work.
Three hundred is the upper weekly figure, not a daily minimum.

items.stem: A poster calls 75 minutes of gentle walking identical to WHO’s 75-minute vigorous option. What is the mix-up?

options.text: It confuses moderate and vigorous intensity.
options.feedback: WHO lists different minute ranges for the two intensities.
A brisk walk can count as moderate activity.

options.text: The figures refer to minutes per month.
options.feedback: WHO states weekly amounts. WHO gives these as amounts for each week.

items.stem: Connect movement to a heart response.

options.text: Muscles work during a brisk walk.
options.feedback: Movement raises their demand. More blood and oxygen are needed as the muscles work.

options.text: The heart pumps blood to support them.
options.feedback: Circulation meets the working muscles. Blood brings oxygen to muscles while they move.
WHO says walks and other moves done often can help the heart.

items.stem: Pair the activity with WHO’s weekly guide.

options.feedback: This is the adult weekly range. WHO uses it for the weekly adult activity guide.
This is the adult weekly range. It is the time range for adults in one week.
Harder work can meet the WHO guide in less time each week.
The vigorous alternative uses fewer minutes. The weekly WHO range is shorter for this kind of work.

misconceptions.name: Only hard sprints count
misconceptions.correction: A brisk walk counts as a form of moderate exercise.

misconceptions.name: Less than 150 minutes is pointless
misconceptions.correction: WHO says some activity is better than none.

sources.title: What's the Link Between Physical Activity and Health?
WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour: at a glance

quest.title: Feel a pulse change
quest.detail: Notice a pulse at rest and after an easy walk. Treat it as a change to observe, not a score.

concepts.title: Iron and anaemia basics
concepts.hook: Beans contain non-haem iron; vitamin C in a meal can help the body absorb that form.
concepts.rule: Iron helps make oxygen-carrying red blood cells. Plant iron is non-haem; vitamin C improves its absorption. Anaemia has several possible causes, so no food example can diagnose it.

claims.text: Vitamin C improves absorption of non-haem iron from plant foods.
Low iron can cause anaemia. Other gaps in food and some infections can cause it too.

items.stem: At a school lunch, lentils supply which form of dietary iron?

options.feedback: Plant foods supply the non-haem form described by NIH.
Lentils have plant iron, called non-haem iron. Haem iron comes from animal foods.

options.text: The same iron that meat gives, taken up just as well.
options.feedback: Lentil iron is the plant kind. The body takes it up less easily than the iron in meat or fish.

items.stem: A college meal pairs beans with a fruit rich in vitamin C. What could the fruit help with?

options.feedback: NIH says vitamin C improves absorption of plant-food iron.
Vitamin C helps the body take in plant iron. It does not turn iron into a new nutrient.
A food combination cannot diagnose a condition. A health test would be needed to tell the cause.

items.stem: Which claim about anaemia fits the WHO guide?

options.text: Iron deficiency is one possible cause.
options.feedback: WHO also lists other deficiencies and infections. So low iron is not the only possible cause.

options.text: Every case is caused only by low iron.
options.feedback: That leaves out other causes WHO names. Low iron is one cause, yet it is not the only one.

options.text: Food choice alone reveals the cause.
options.feedback: A meal cannot tell the cause of a person’s anaemia. There are other causes too.

items.stem: Why does NIH distinguish haem from non-haem iron?

options.text: They differ in absorption and response to other foods.
options.feedback: Vitamin C can help the body take in plant iron, the non-haem form.

options.text: Only haem iron can support red blood cells.
options.feedback: Non-haem iron is still dietary iron. The body can still use iron from plant foods.

options.text: Plant iron disappears when eaten with fruit.
options.feedback: Vitamin C can help the body take in more plant iron. It does not block it.

items.stem: For iron from a mixed diet with meat, seafood and vitamin C, what lower end of the NIH absorption range applies, in percent?

options.feedback: NIH gives roughly 14–18% for such mixed diets.
Five is the lower end of its vegetarian-diet range.
That is far above the range NIH reports.

items.stem: A page says a person with anaemia must simply eat more beans. What is the problem?

options.text: Anaemia can have causes beyond low iron.
options.feedback: WHO names other nutrient gaps, infections and blood loss.
Beans can supply non-haem iron; that does not settle a diagnosis.
Better iron uptake does not show the cause of anaemia. It does not treat all causes.

items.stem: Trace a supported food-and-iron link.

options.feedback: Beans and lentils contain this form. That iron can help the body make haemoglobin.

options.text: Vitamin C can improve its absorption.
options.feedback: NIH describes this food interaction. This can help the body take in more plant iron.
Iron helps make haemoglobin. Red blood cells use it to carry oxygen.

items.stem: Pair the term with its meaning.

options.feedback: NIH describes this form in plants. Beans and lentils are plant foods that supply it.
NIH describes this form in plants. This is the iron form found in beans and lentils.
It affects uptake, not diagnosis. It can help with plant iron, yet cannot name an illness.
It affects uptake, not diagnosis. Food uptake does not show why a person has anaemia.

misconceptions.name: All iron is absorbed alike
misconceptions.correction: Haem and non-haem iron differ in absorption.

misconceptions.name: All anaemia is low iron
misconceptions.correction: Anaemia can have more than one cause, such as low iron or an infection.

sources.title: Vitamin C: Health Professional Fact Sheet

quest.title: Find food sources
quest.detail: Look at a meal and name any beans, nuts or other foods listed as iron sources.

concepts.title: Reading a food label
concepts.hook: Two packs can use different serving sizes; a per-100-g line gives the same comparison base.
concepts.rule: Compare like foods on their per-100-g or per-100-ml lines. A serving may differ by pack, and ingredients are listed from greatest to least weight.

claims.text: NHS says nutrition values are given per 100 g or 100 ml and may also be given per portion.
Packaged-food ingredients are listed in descending order by weight.

items.stem: At a canteen, two biscuits have different serving sizes. Which line gives a fair same weight comparison?

options.feedback: NHS says that base is common across labels.
Different serving weights make those numbers hard to compare.

options.text: The first name in the ingredients list.
options.feedback: That list shows order by weight, not amounts you can compare. The per-100-g line puts both packs on one base.

items.stem: At a family shop, one cereal lists sugar first among its ingredients. What does that position mean?

options.text: Sugar is the greatest ingredient by weight.
options.feedback: NHS says ingredients run in descending weight order.

options.text: Sugar is present in the smallest amount.
options.feedback: That reverses the stated ordering rule. The first item has the most weight in the mix.

options.text: The cereal must have no other ingredients.
options.feedback: First does not mean only. There can still be more items later in the list.

items.stem: Which pair of label lines should be compared for two drinks?

options.text: The same nutrient per 100 ml on both.
options.feedback: Using the same amount gives a like-for-like base.

options.text: One per serving and one per 100 ml.
options.feedback: The bases differ and can distort the comparison.

options.text: Only the front picture on each bottle.
options.feedback: Pictures do not state comparable nutrient amounts. The back label gives amounts that can be checked.

items.stem: Why can a lower salt value per serving hide a higher salt concentration?

options.feedback: A smaller portion can contain less salt despite more per 100 g.

options.text: A serving is always exactly 100 g.
options.feedback: Labels can state other serving sizes. A pack may define one serving as more or less.

options.text: Salt is never shown per 100 g.
options.feedback: NHS describes per-100-g nutrition information. That line helps compare the same mass of two foods.

items.stem: When reading a food label, above how many grams of salt per 100 g does NHS call a food high in salt?

options.feedback: That is the NHS high-salt cutoff for food.
That is near the low-salt boundary, not the high cutoff.
This adds a zero to the NHS threshold.

items.stem: A pack says “small serving” while the shopper eats twice that amount. What changes?

options.text: The per-serving nutrient amount must be scaled.
options.feedback: A label may call one small amount a serving. A person may eat more.
If you eat more, you take in more in all. The amount per 100 g stays the same.
Ingredient order is based on product weight, not portion chosen.

items.stem: Compare two packaged foods fairly.

options.text: Find the same nutrient on each pack.
options.feedback: Compare salt with salt, for example. This keeps the kind of nutrient the same.
This removes serving-size differences. It lets the two packs be compared on equal weight.

options.text: Read the values and portion context.
options.feedback: The amount eaten can differ from the stated serving.

items.stem: Pair the label feature with its meaning.

options.feedback: Both packs refer to the same mass. The same mass makes amounts fair to compare.
Both packs refer to the same mass. A common weight base helps compare two packs.
The list descends by ingredient weight. The first item makes up the most by weight.
The list descends by ingredient weight. The order tells which item weighs more in the mix.

misconceptions.name: Serving sizes are universal
misconceptions.correction: Two food packs may use different sizes for one serving.

misconceptions.name: First ingredient is smallest
misconceptions.correction: The first listed ingredient has the greatest weight.

quest.title: Compare two labels
quest.detail: Look at two similar packs and find the same per-100 g or per-100 ml line on each.

concepts.title: Fad diet claims
concepts.hook: A “detox” menu promises a special clean-out, yet the body already has organs that process waste.
concepts.rule: A varied diet supplies different nutrients. Be wary of single-food and detox claims; no one food covers every need, and the liver does not need a special detox diet.

claims.text: ICMR-NIN says to eat from many food groups. No one food gives all the key nutrients.
An NHS source says the liver does not need a detox diet; WHO gives a 400-g fruit-and-vegetable guide for people over ten.

items.stem: A college diet plan allows only one food for every meal. Which claim is weakest?

options.text: That one food can supply every needed nutrient.
options.feedback: ICMR-NIN stresses variety because foods differ. One food cannot meet every need on its own.

options.text: That the food may contain some nutrients.
options.feedback: One food may help. It still cannot meet all the body’s needs alone.

options.text: That a mix of foods brings different nutrients.
options.feedback: That claim is well supported. Food groups differ, so a mix fills gaps one food leaves.

items.stem: A school poster says a special juice week is required to detox the liver. What is the sound response?

options.text: The liver does not need a detox diet.
options.feedback: The NHS source rejects that requirement. The liver already does this work without a special diet.

options.text: Juice contains no free sugar at all.
options.feedback: WHO counts juice sugars as free sugars. Juice sugars still count under the WHO free sugar rule.

options.text: A juice-only menu guarantees nutrient variety.
options.feedback: Removing food groups works against variety. A narrow menu can leave out key food groups.

items.stem: Which pattern best matches ICMR-NIN’s balanced-diet approach?

options.text: A variety of food groups over time.
options.feedback: Different groups contribute different nutrients. That mix helps cover needs one group may miss.
A single food cannot cover all nutrient needs.

options.text: Avoiding every cereal because all carbs are harmful.
options.feedback: The guide counts grains and millets as part of a varied mix of foods.

items.stem: Why is “all carbohydrates are bad” a poor reading of a varied-diet guide?

options.text: It lumps useful cereals, pulses and other foods into one ban.
options.feedback: ICMR-NIN includes these groups as part of balanced eating.
Foods differ in nutrient mix and context. Two foods can differ in what else they supply.

options.text: Avoiding all plant foods improves variety.
options.feedback: That removes many food groups rather than broadening them.

items.stem: When you check a fad diet claim, how many grams of fruit and veg a day does WHO advise for people older than ten?

options.feedback: WHO gives 400 g as the adult and older-child guide.
That drops a zero from the WHO amount.
That adds a zero and is not the WHO guide.

items.stem: A claim says a single vegetable can replace pulses, grains and every other group. What is missing?

options.feedback: Variety is the point of the ICMR-NIN guidance.
Veg can help, yet it does not meet all needs on its own.

options.text: Every pulse and cereal has the same profile.
options.feedback: The two foods have different mixes. That is why they can help fill each other’s gaps.

items.stem: Check a sweeping food claim.

options.text: Read exactly what the ad promises.
options.feedback: A “one food does all” claim needs scrutiny.
Variety supplies different nutrients. That is why a plan with one food is too narrow.

options.text: Compare the claim with a trusted guide.
options.feedback: The ICMR-NIN guide gives the broader pattern.

items.stem: Pair each claim with the evidence-based response.

options.feedback: The varied-diet guide rejects a single-food answer.
The varied-diet guide rejects a single-food answer.

options.text: A special detox diet is required
options.feedback: The NHS source rejects the supposed requirement. The liver does its work without a juice cleanse.

options.text: The liver does not need one
options.feedback: The NHS source rejects the supposed requirement. No special juice plan is needed for the liver.

misconceptions.name: One food can cover all needs
misconceptions.correction: Food groups differ. Each can bring in nutrients that others have less of.

misconceptions.name: Detox menu repairs the liver
misconceptions.correction: A special detox diet is not needed for normal liver function.
